text: What is left, most important first.

Problem 20.84 itself: is $D_5(Q)=1$ for all finite $2$-groups of class $3$? A counterexample must have $D_4(Q)\ne1$ and order $\ge2^{12}$; at order $2^{12}$ it is a candidate of rank $\le8$. (For $D_4\ne\gamma_4$ alone the bound is $2^{11}$; the smallest known example has order $2^{38}$.) Tracker: D5-2

Is there $3$-torsion in $D_5/\gamma_5$, i.e. is Tahara's bound $6$ attained? A minimal example has order $\ge3^{10}$, class $4$, cyclic centre, $\gamma_2/\gamma_3$ of exponent $\ge9$ (hence at least two invariants $\ge9$ in $Q/\gamma_2$) and $\gamma_4\le Z(Q)$ cyclic; $\gamma_4\cong C_3$ or $C_9$ when the second largest invariant of $Q/\gamma_2$ is $9$ (Theorem 6.9). Tracker: D5-4

Is $D_5=\gamma_5$ for finite $3$-groups with $\gamma_2/\gamma_3$ of exponent $\ge9$ (this needs at least two invariants $\ge9$ in $Q/\gamma_2$, e.g. $C_9\times C_9\times C_3$)? With exponent $3$, $D_5=\gamma_5$ whatever the invariants (Theorem 6.9). A minimal counterexample has class $4$, cyclic centre and $\gamma_4\le Z(Q)$ cyclic, with $\gamma_4\cong C_3$ or $C_9$ when the second largest invariant of $Q/\gamma_2$ is $9$. With exponent $9$ the proof breaks in several places; e.g. the exact class-$4$ formula is $[x^3,a]=[x,a]^3[x,a,x]^3$, and in $\langle x,y\mid x^9,y^9\rangle/\gamma_5$ one has $[x,a,x]^3\ne1$ (Remark 6.7). Tracker: D5-49
The group analogue of Theorem C: $D_{2c-1}(G)=1$ for metabelian groups of class $\le c$? For odd primes the answer is yes for every $c$ (Gupta, 1991); open for $p=2$, $c\ge3$. Tracker: D5-7

Central products glued along a proper subgroup when $\sigma$ is not a $2^{j+1}$-th power: $12$ of the $212$ splittings of candidates of orders $2^8$–$2^9$ are covered by nothing. A projection to $H$ cannot do it in general: for $D_8\circ_{\langle t\rangle}M_{16}$ the ring equality fails at $n=4,5$. Tracker: D5-8
